1037.title: Punjab's drug crisis
1037.hook: families and gurdwaras are working to help young people out of addiction
1037.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to avoid intoxicants. Some gurdwaras and Sikh organizations in Punjab and abroad support recovery work, youth programs and families facing addiction, alongside medical treatment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, caste, honestly, and your line was the gurus rejected it. Today, another hard subject, met the same way: with the lights on.

A mother sits on the steps outside a gurdwara, holding her son's phone. He asked her to keep it. He's a few days into trying to stop, and he doesn't trust himself with the numbers saved inside. Through the doors, kirtan is playing. A volunteer brings her a cup of tea and sits down beside her without asking a single question. In Punjab, families have been living stories like this, and talking about them at kitchen tables, in songs and in the gurdwara. Today isn't about blame. It's about the hands reaching in.
screen: `A MOTHER HOLDS HER SON'S PHONE.` → `TEA, AND NO QUESTIONS.` → `THE HANDS REACHING IN.`

segments.voice: Addiction in Punjab has reached into homes: a son, a cousin, a classmate, a neighbor's boy who used to play cricket in the lane. There are figures, and people argue about them. This lesson leaves them out, because behind every one is a person with a name. At Ang 554 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Amar Das describes what the false wine does: drinking it, a person loses their sense, can't tell their own from a stranger, and is pushed away from the Master. So, he says, don't drink this false wine at all, if it is in your power. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, carries the same teaching: it asks Sikhs to keep away from intoxicants, and names liquor, tobacco, opium and hemp among them. But the salok doesn't stop at the warning. It speaks of a true wine, found by grace, by the one who meets the True Guru. It doesn't only take something away; it points to something to fill the empty place. Then the hands. Families, doctors and sangats work on this together. Some gurdwaras and Sikh groups support recovery programs, sports for young people and kirtan classes. Some sangats have learned to sit with a family instead of whispering about it. Shame keeps people hidden. A sangat that pulls up a chair makes it easier to come out. Not lecture them out. Not shame them out. Help them out.
screen: `ADDICTION HAS REACHED INTO HOMES.` · `ANG 554: DON'T DRINK THE FALSE WINE.` · `A TRUE WINE, FOUND BY GRACE.` · `FAMILIES, DOCTORS AND SANGATS.` · then, large: `HELP THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: Go back to the gurdwara steps and take the volunteer's place: a cup of tea in your hands, beside someone carrying something heavy, maybe the mother, maybe someone you know who is struggling with a drink, a drug, a screen, grief, or something they haven't told anyone. Don't speak and don't fix anything; feel the warmth of the cup and keep your place on the step, because sitting there is the whole job. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Nasha. Intoxication, the addiction that has reached into Punjabi homes, with families, gurdwaras and doctors working to bring young people out of it. Today's word.
Your line: help them out. And if someone is in danger, get them to a doctor or emergency help first. See you tomorrow.

1038.title: Choosing the turban
1038.hook: young Sikhs decide for themselves how to keep kesh and turban
1038.howItsDone: Sikhs who take amrit keep kesh, uncut hair, as one of the five articles of faith, and Sikh men and some Sikh women cover it with a turban. Some young Sikhs begin with a patka and decide for themselves when to tie a full turban.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nasha, and your line was help them out. Today, young Sikhs again, and a choice that's theirs to make.

Sunday morning. A teenager stands at the bathroom mirror with a long strip of cloth over one shoulder and a phone propped against the tap, playing a tying tutorial at half speed. Fold, wrap, pin, start again. Down the hall, a younger brother still wears a patka, the small cloth their mother ties for him each morning. The teenager could have kept the patka, or stopped covering at all. Instead, the cloth goes round once more, and this morning, it holds.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH AND A TUTORIAL.` → `FOLD, WRAP, PIN, AGAIN.` → `THIS MORNING, IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles of faith. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs who have taken amrit to keep their hair uncut, and the turban covers and honors it. Young Sikhs come to this in different ways. Some grow up in a patka and move to a full turban. Some girls choose a turban, or a keski, a smaller one. Some cut their hair for years and later grow it back. Families argue about it, pray about it, and still sit down to dinner. The gurdwara door stays open to all of them. Why does choice matter? Tradition remembers the day Guru Gobind Singh called the Khalsa into being: he asked who would come forward, and one by one, five did. And the Rehat Maryada asks that those who take amrit be old enough to understand what they're promising. The Khalsa begins with a person stepping forward. Today the choice can mean first tries that come out lopsided. Ask Sikhs about a first turban and you hear kind words: looks good; practice makes perfect; nobody should judge your pagg at the gurdwara. Many start with a simpler style and grow into it. It can mean wearing a turban to a new school, a job interview or a sports field, and answering the same question politely, again and again. It can mean waiting until you're sure. Some Sikhs put it this way: a turban tied because you chose it becomes a promise you keep.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who chose something you might not have chosen: what they wear, what they believe, what they gave up or took on. Breathe in and picture them making that decision, maybe at a mirror, maybe late at night; breathe out and let go of the urge to vote on it, because it's theirs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Kesh. Uncut hair, which young Sikhs choose for themselves how to keep and whether and how to cover with a turban, a choice the tradition wants made with understanding. Today's word.
Your line: their choice. Understanding comes first, before any verdict. Day one thousand thirty-eight, done.

1039.title: Gurmukhi on screens
1039.hook: the Granth is now searchable online, with translations
1039.howItsDone: Sikhs use websites and apps to search the Guru Granth Sahib by ang or by the first letters of a line, and some gurdwaras project the hymn being sung in Gurmukhi with a transliteration and a translation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kesh, and your line was their choice. Today, the phone screen gets a bigger job: carrying the Guru's word.

At the back of a gurdwara, a girl leans toward her grandfather and whispers: what's that line? The ragis are singing, and she can't quite catch it. He doesn't open a book. He points at the wall, where a screen shows the line in Gurmukhi, then the same sounds in Roman letters, then a meaning in English. He reads the top line. She reads the bottom two, mouthing the words. For a moment they're singing the same hymn from different ends of the screen.
screen: `WHAT'S THAT LINE?` → `GURMUKHI, SOUNDS, MEANING.` → `ONE HYMN, TWO ENDS OF A SCREEN.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib is read by ang, the word Sikhs use for its pages. Printed copies keep the same page layout, which is why these lessons can send you to one ang and you'll find the same hymn there. Today the whole Granth can be searched on a phone or a website. Some tools let you type just the first letter of each word, so a half-remembered line can still be found. In some gurdwaras, the line being sung goes up on a screen with a transliteration and a translation, so someone who can't read Gurmukhi can follow along. One careful step, though. Sikhs treat the Gurmukhi as the Guru's own word. A translation underneath is a helper: one person's reading, made with care, but not the Guru. Different translations sometimes disagree, and that's a reason to go back to the top line, not away from it. At Ang 982, Guru Ram Das says it plainly: bani guru, guru hai bani. The Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and within the Word is all the nectar. For Sikhs who hold that, a screen that carries the Word into the back row can be a kind of seva: a lamp moved closer to people who couldn't see. Not a replacement for the Granth. A way to reach it.
screen: `READ BY ANG, THE SAME PAGES.` · `SEARCH BY FIRST LETTERS.` · `A TRANSLATION IS A HELPER.` · `BANI GURU, GURU HAI BANI.` · then, large: `THE WORD ONLINE.`

segments.voice: If you have a screen nearby, open any ang of the Guru Granth Sahib and pick one line; if not, use today's: bani guru, guru hai bani. Breathe in with the first half and out with the second, and sit with what it means, the Word is the Guru, without hurrying to the next line. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.
Gurmukhi. The script of the Guru Granth Sahib, now searchable online and shown on screens with transliteration and translation, so more people can reach the Word itself. Today's word.
Your line: the word online. The top line stays the Guru's own word. Until tomorrow.

1040.title: Is that really a photo?
1040.hook: the Gurus lived long before cameras; every picture of a Guru is an artist's work, and some online images are made up
1040.howItsDone: Paintings and prints of the Gurus hang in many Sikh homes and are loved as art; Sikh teaching holds that God is formless and that pictures are not to be worshiped, and no photograph of any Guru exists, since the Gurus lived from 1469 to 1708 and photography began in the 1820s.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, and your line was the word online. Today, what else the screen carries, and how to tell.

A message lands in a family group chat: an old, brown-tinted photograph of a man with a white beard and a gentle face, captioned in capital letters, rare real photo of Guru Nanak. Folded hands and hearts fill the replies. An aunt forwards it to three more groups. Then a teenager types one line: cameras weren't invented until the eighteen-twenties. The chat goes very quiet.
screen: `A FAMILY GROUP CHAT.` → `RARE REAL PHOTO OF GURU NANAK.` → `CAMERAS CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: The ten Gurus lived from 1469 to 1708. The first lasting photographs were made in the 1820s, more than a century after the tenth Guru died. So there is no photograph of any Guru. What gets shared as one is a painting, a modern actor in costume, or, more and more, an image a computer program made in seconds. Sikh painting itself is old and much loved: scenes painted into janamsakhi manuscripts, portraits made in the Punjab hills and at Lahore, prints on the walls of countless homes. Many help people feel close to the Gurus, and there's nothing wrong with loving them. But each is an artist's picture, mostly made long after the Guru lived, and no one can be sure what any Guru looked like. That matters more here. Sikh teaching calls God nirankar, the formless, and the Guru now is the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word. Pictures are not to be worshiped. So a painting can be treasured as a painting, without anyone claiming it's a likeness. Sikhs themselves have been asking for a habit lately: check the date, ask who made it, and say painting when it's a painting. Guru Nanak kept asking gentle questions, like why throw water toward the sun? Asking isn't disrespect.
screen: `THE GURUS: 1469 TO 1708.` · `CAMERAS: THE 1820S.` · `LOVED ART, NOT A LIKENESS.` · `CHECK, ASK, SAY PAINTING.` · then, large: `A PAINTING, NOT A PHOTO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an image of a Guru you've seen, on a wall, a calendar or a phone, and hold it with affection, letting it give you what it gives: warmth, closeness, a face to turn toward. Breathe out and say gently, inside, someone painted this, with love, long after, and notice that nothing is lost: the love stays, and the facts settle into place. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Tasveer. A picture, a portrait. Every tasveer of a Guru is an artist's work, made long after; none is a photograph. Today's word.
Your line: a painting, not a photo. Love the art, and keep the facts straight. That's day one thousand forty.

1041.title: Cleaning a river
1041.hook: volunteers cleaned the Kali Bein, the river where Nanak disappeared, by kar seva
1041.howItsDone: Kar seva is volunteer labor for a sacred place, such as cleaning a gurdwara's sarovar or building and repairing gurdwaras. At Sultanpur Lodhi, volunteers have cleaned the Kali Bein by kar seva, and Sikhs visit the Gurdwara Ber Sahib there, linked with the story of Guru Nanak's disappearance in the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tasveer, and your line was a painting, not a photo. Today, something old comes back to life, and this time it's a river.

Mud up to the knees. A line of volunteers stands in a narrow, choked stream, passing buckets of black silt and tangled weeds from hand to hand up the bank. Some are farmers, some are students, some came after work. Nobody is paid. The water barely moves, and it smells. But the stories of Guru Nanak know this stream. It's the Kali Bein, at Sultanpur Lodhi, where, the stories say, Nanak went into the water and vanished.
screen: `MUD TO THE KNEES.` → `BUCKETS UP THE BANK.` → `THE KALI BEIN.`

segments.voice: The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak, tell of the morning he went to bathe in the Bein and vanished. Tradition says he was gone for three days, and that when he came back, his first words were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. This path told that story long ago. Today, the river itself. In our own times the Kali Bein was choked with weeds and waste, and dirty water ran into it. The river of that story was hard to recognize. Then volunteers began to clean it by kar seva, the Sikh name for free, hands-on work for a sacred place, the same kind of work that has cleaned the pools at gurdwaras. A Sikh sant, Balbir Singh Seechewal, is known for leading it. They cleared weeds and silt by hand, worked on stopping the dirty water, and planted the banks. Over time, the water ran again. The root is in the Asa di Var, at Ang 472, where Guru Nanak says that first of all, water is life, by which everything is made green. If water is where life begins, a dirty river isn't only an eyesore. It's a wound in the place the Guru called life itself. So the volunteers treated it as seva, not a project. The Guru disappeared into that water. They made sure there was water worth coming back out of.
screen: `NANAK VANISHED INTO THE BEIN.` · `THE RIVER CHOKED WITH WASTE.` · `KAR SEVA, BUCKET BY BUCKET.` · `FIRST, WATER IS LIFE.` · then, large: `CLEAN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: If you can, set a glass of water in front of you and look at it. Breathe in and think of where it came from, a river, a reservoir, rain on a hillside far away; breathe out and think of where it goes next, downstream to someone else, a field, a fish. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and then take one slow sip.
Kali Bein. The river at Sultanpur Lodhi where tradition says Guru Nanak disappeared and came back with his first teaching, cleared by volunteers through kar seva. Today's word.
Your line: clean the river. First of all, the Guru says, water is life. See you tomorrow.

1042.title: Planting forests
1042.hook: Sikh groups plant small forests to honor Guru Nanak
1042.howItsDone: Some Sikh organizations and sangats plant small, dense forests of native trees near gurdwaras, schools and villages in honor of Guru Nanak, and Sikhs recite the Japji's closing salok, which names air, water and earth as Guru, father and mother.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kali Bein, and your line was clean the river. Today the volunteers climb out of the river and pick up shovels.

A scrap of land behind a village school: hard dirt, a broken wall, a pile of bricks nobody moved. A sangat arrives after the Sunday program with saplings in plastic bags, a cart of compost, and a list of trees that belong to this soil. They don't plant in neat rows. They plant close, shoulder to shoulder, the way a real forest grows, and children press the earth down around each stem. A few seasons later, that scrap of dirt is a green wall full of birds. It was planted for one person.
screen: `A SCRAP OF HARD DIRT.` → `SAPLINGS SHOULDER TO SHOULDER.` → `A GREEN WALL OF BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Sikh groups have been planting small, dense forests in honor of Guru Nanak, on patches of land near gurdwaras, schools, farms and villages. Some call them Guru Nanak sacred forests. Instead of a few big trees far apart, they plant native trees and shrubs close together, so they compete for light and grow fast and thick. Some groups use a way of planting that comes from Japan. The point is a real forest on a small plot, not a park. The root is a short salok at Ang 8, which Sikhs who recite the Japji in the morning say at its end. In Gurmukhi it begins: pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother. So a forest isn't decoration. It's family: the ones the salok names as teacher and parents. There's an old green thread, too. Tradition remembers Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, keeping gardens and growing healing herbs, and tells of him as a boy brushing a flower with his robe and breaking it, and taking care with every living thing after that. The forests carry that thread forward. A tree planted for Nanak gives shade to anyone, of any faith, who sits under it, and gives the great mother back a little of what was taken.

segments.voice: Breathe in and notice the air, the Guru, the salok says; feel your feet on the floor and the earth below it, the great mother; think of the water inside you, the father. Stay with whichever one is easiest to feel. If you pray, you can say pavan guru, pani pita, mata dharat mahat once, slowly.

Your line: a forest for nanak. A small plot can still hold a forest. Day one thousand forty-two, planted.

1043.title: The kitchen at Amritsar
1043.hook: the langar at the Golden Temple feeds tens of thousands every day
1043.howItsDone: At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the langar serves free vegetarian meals to all visitors, who sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor; volunteers cook, serve and wash the dishes as seva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, planting forests, and your line was a forest for nanak. Today, from the forest to a kitchen in Amritsar.

The sound comes first: steel plates, stacked and passed and clattering, a rolling metal river of them. Then the smell: lentils, butter, fresh roti. Then the hall itself, at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, also called the Golden Temple. People sit on long strips of matting, row after row: a farmer, a tourist with a camera, a businessman, a grandmother, a child. A volunteer walks down the row with a bucket of dal, ladling the same amount onto every plate. Nobody asks who you are.
screen: `A RIVER OF STEEL PLATES.` → `ROW AFTER ROW ON THE FLOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: The gurdwara's own accounts say its langar feeds tens of thousands of people every day, and more on festival days. The food is free. Volunteers do much of the work: kneading dough, rolling roti, stirring huge pots, washing plates. The sitting in rows is called pangat. Everyone eats at the same level, the same food, from the same kitchen. There is no head table, and no better plate for an important guest. Tradition tells that when the emperor Akbar came to meet Guru Amar Das, he was asked to do what everyone did first: sit in the pangat and eat langar. Sikhs sum up the old rule in a short phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat. First the row, then the gathering. A ruler of an empire, the story goes, sat on the floor beside whoever was there. After the meal comes the washing. Visitors line up to scrub steel next to students and farmers. The hands get wrinkled, the plates go back out, and the river keeps flowing. Tens of thousands fed is not a statistic. It's a meal, multiplied, and every plate given the same.
screen: `FREE FOOD, CARRIED BY VOLUNTEERS.` · `PANGAT: EVERYONE IN THE SAME ROW.` · `FIRST THE ROW, THEN THE GATHERING.` · `WASHING THE PLATES.` · then, large: `TENS OF THOUSANDS FED.`

segments.voice: Picture the hall and the long mats, and put yourself in the row: a stranger on your left, another on your right, and the plate landing in front of you the same as theirs. Breathe in, receiving; breathe out, and picture yourself at the sinks, washing someone else's plate. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Pangat. The row where everyone sits together to eat, at the Harmandir Sahib's langar in Amritsar, with free meals served to everyone who comes. Today's word.

Your line: tens of thousands fed. That ends a week of Sikh life now: help out of addiction, a turban chosen, the word on screens, honest pictures, a clean river, a forest, and this kitchen. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.
